script: Got my doctorate. My stepdad has a much larger age gap with his siblings, which makes my aunt about the same age as me. She crushed it, earned a Ph.D. in veterinary medicine, and I am just like, "Nice." But here's the thing—my own degree was a Master of Social Work, and I was juggling a million things at the time. I snagged that MSW because it was the ticket to my career, and honestly, I didn't need more than that. What I didn't know was that my life was about to get a whole lot more complicated. I had a dad, a stepdad, a grandma, a grandpa, a bunch of cousins—everyone was a puzzle piece that suddenly needed a new fit. Fast forward a few years, and my grandpa, a veteran, gets diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. The doctor said, "You're going to need a team." I was the only one who knew the VA, Medicare, and the maze of home health services. If I didn't pull this together, he'd be drowning in paperwork and I'd lose my credibility. The stakes? If I didn't manage it, I'd lose everything—my career, my family's trust, that whole "good kid" vibe. I couldn't even sleep at night. In the middle of all this, my aunt starts arguing with me. She's like, "You need a Doctor title to be in charge." She was already fighting her dad's wishes, and now she's throwing her weight around, making the situation a mess. I could feel my patience draining. And that's when everything changed—she had the audacity to say the word "doctor" as if it was a badge of authority over the VA system. I finally snapped. "You know what? I am going to get my doctorate just to spite her." I told the family, and my grandpa, who was proud, bragged about it to everyone. He was the emotional anchor, and I needed to show him that I could earn that title, not just for the prestige but for the power to advocate for him. But here's the thing—earning a doctorate isn't just about the title; it's about proving that I am better equipped than the people who're trying to control me. So I dove into the Doctor of Social Work program. The coursework was brutal, the exams were a nightmare, and I was juggling the grandpa's care. Every late-night study session felt like a battle. If I failed, my grandpa would be left with no advocate, and the whole system would swallow him whole. I could feel my heart pounding, my stomach dropping, and my confidence wavering. But what I didn't know was that the hardest part wasn't the exams—it was the emotional toll of watching my grandpa's condition worsen while trying to keep my own life afloat. Finally, the day came. I walked across that stage, a cap and gown that felt heavier than any of my old shoes. I saw my grandpa in the audience, eyes wet, and I knew this was the moment I'd promised him. My doctorate, my DSW, was not just a piece of paper. It was a shield. And that's when everything changed—the room was silent, and I felt like I had just won a war. But here's the thing—this victory was bittersweet, because the real battle was still ahead. After graduation, I stayed with my grandpa until the end. I managed his appointments, fought for better care, and made sure he had the dignity he deserved. He looked at me, proud, and whispered, "You did it, kid." I held his hand, and I knew that the title mattered less than the trust we built. But what happened next? That part nobody saw coming—he was suddenly in a sudden crisis, and I had to act fast. The next move? I have no idea, but I am ready.
